content:
Have you ever turned on the radio and felt that every pop song sounds the same? Or watched a horror film and figured out the ending after just 20 minutes?

Researchers from the Singapore Management University and James Cook University Singapore, in a new paper published in *Frontiers in Psychology*, argue that "hyper-selection" refers to how, when competition becomes intense, we become increasingly adept at identifying and optimising what works, and we keep selecting for the same kinds of traits rather than trying anything else.

The result is a dampening of creativity. In a world that increasingly demands optimisation, "hyper-selection" could end up making everything from music to urban planning to football matches more boring.

Jose C. Yong, a research psychologist and the paper's first author, likens "hyper-selection" to natural selection — the evolutionary process in which certain individuals are more likely to survive and reproduce because they possess advantageous traits or more effective strategies. Modern technology has made this selection process extraordinarily fast and intense.

"We can now instantly identify what is performing the best, almost immediately copy it, and then keep optimising it," Yong said. "This process accelerates when there are strong selection pressures — for example, intense competition, or when the consequences of not optimising are severe."

Optimisation is usually useful, because it helps us achieve our goals more efficiently. But when everyone is optimising for the same thing, other traits, behaviours, products and strategies may gradually disappear, "trading away diversity or variability — which might themselves have been adaptively valuable and useful — in exchange for efficiency."

When we fall into "hyper-selection", we miss out on creative masterworks like 'Bohemian Rhapsody'

When explaining the concept of "hyper-selection" to people unfamiliar with it, Yong likes to use Queen's "Bohemian Rhapsody" as an example. Critics in 1975 initially panned the song as an "audacious pastiche" and a "stylistic hodgepodge", but the single is now regarded as one of the greatest rock tracks of all time, largely because the band was willing to take creative risks.

"Bohemian Rhapsody is the opposite of hyper-selection."

"The song is nearly six minutes long, transitions between wildly different musical sections, has no traditional chorus, and features a famous operatic passage," Yong said.

Another work that clearly does not fall under "hyper-selection" is Stevie Nicks's "Edge of Seventeen", which breaks conventional song structures yet has a distinctive sound that is instantly recognisable. Yong also points to System of a Down, whose songs he says sound "outrageously weird" yet still managed to top the charts, "because their music is fresh and distinctive enough".

Compared with the past, today's radio hits often lack originality and feel boring — Yong even struggles to pick out a single example.

"Honestly, I'm not sure I can name a current pop song that exemplifies hyper-selection. Part of it is that so much pop music now sounds too similar, with no single track standing out," he said.

But he says some music genres are saturated with "hyper-selection" — for instance, the moody, melancholic pop songs where singers murmur in breathy vocals, or the mumble-rap that was everywhere a few years ago.

Yong's co-author and fellow research psychologist Edison Tan has also all but stopped listening to the radio because of "hyper-selection", turning instead to discovering emerging, less-played independent artists.

"It's not that my taste has changed — it's that the world has," Tan told *HuffPost*. "What I crave is rich and nuanced emotional expression, and pop music no longer delivers that."

Yong says that, driven by metrics such as streaming data, marketing value and the fleeting attention spans of social media, the music industry has seen a well-documented trend of songs getting shorter and simpler in structure.

Beyond music, where else does "hyper-selection" show up?

Yong, Tan and their co-author Simon S. Groome argue that "hyper-selection" — the pursuit of optimisation and efficiency — is making nearly every layer of our lives more predictable, bland and boring. They see it in the world of sport as well.

In professional football, teams are constantly searching for tactics that can give them an edge. When a particular strategy proves successful, rivals quickly follow suit. Matches become more intense and tactics more sophisticated, but teams are also playing in increasingly similar ways, leaving less room for individual flair.

Our working lives are no exception. Tan points to academia, a world he knows well.

"When we were graduate students, we were taught to dare to innovate, to explore new ideas, to probe how the world works," he said.

In an ideal world, the best researchers would be the most creative problem-solvers — those bold enough to blaze their own trails. But reality falls far short of these ideals.

"Scholars are forced to prove their worth through metrics like publication counts, citation numbers and how much research funding they bring in — not by the value of the ideas themselves," Tan said.

He added: "The P for Philosophy in a PhD has long disappeared. When we start seeing the same pattern emerge in every layer of our lives, it's hard not to wonder whether some fundamental force is driving these trends."

Artificial intelligence will speed up "hyper-selection"

It almost goes without saying that artificial intelligence will accelerate "hyper-selection", Yong says. AI is, by design, constantly and recursively optimising itself with little need for human input, and it operates at a speed and scale far beyond what humans — or any previous technology — can match.

"We're already seeing this in online content — AI-generated articles, marketing copy, social media posts, images, videos, web design and even music all feel startlingly similar, because they're generated from the same underlying patterns and increasingly optimised for what works," he said.

If people accept this content uncritically, there will be little force to push back against the AI-driven "hyper-selection".

"Hyper-selection" is not entirely bad, but creators need to be aware of it.

Yong stresses that optimisation is not inherently a bad thing — it can help people achieve their goals and improve their lives. But because the pressure to optimise can be intense, creators may unwittingly sacrifice adaptively valuable variation.

"That's why being aware of 'hyper-selection' is important, and part of why I want to spell the concept out clearly — because once we can recognise it, we can think about how to respond when it happens," he said.

Yong says the key is to recognise how easily we fall into the trap of "hyper-selection", and to find ways to nurture creativity and preserve diversity.

"Creativity often comes from exposure to different things and recombining them in new ways. If everything starts to look, sound and function the same, we lose the reservoir of alternative strategies — the raw material from which new ideas can spring," he said.

We also need to be more deliberate about what we consume.

"If audiences can learn to recognise when music, films or other cultural products become overly formulaic, and demand something more interesting, that alone can shift the selection pressures acting on what gets produced," Yong said.
